Message Type: FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: /root
Sender: /root/sol_discovery_b
Payload:
## Candidate: one grounded matrix for both directional hitting times

For a connected simple unweighted graph \(G=(V,E)\), distinct \(s,t\), \(m=|E|\), degree vector \(d\), and combinatorial Laplacian \(L=D-A\), let

\[
R=V\setminus\{t\},\qquad A_t=L[R,R].
\]

Solve the two-right-hand-side exact system

\[
A_t
\begin{bmatrix}
x & y
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
d_R & (d-2m e_s)_R
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Extend both columns with \(x_t=y_t=0\). Then

\[
H_{s\to t}=x_s,\qquad H_{t\to s}=-y_s.
\]

The full reverse hitting-time vector is \(h^{(s)}=y-y_s\mathbf1\).

### Proof

For destination \(q\), first-step equations give

\[
h^{(q)}_q=0,\qquad
h^{(q)}_v=1+\frac1{d_v}\sum_{w\sim v}h^{(q)}_w
\quad(v\ne q).
\]

Multiplying by \(d_v\) yields \((Lh^{(q)})_v=d_v\) for \(v\ne q\). Since every Laplacian row sums to zero,

\[
Lh^{(q)}=d-2m e_q.
\]

Connectedness makes every grounded principal minor \(A_t\) nonsingular.

For \(q=t\), deleting row and column \(t\) gives \(A_tx=d_R\), so \(x=h^{(t)}\) and \(x_s=H_{s\to t}\).

For \(q=s\), \(y_t=0\) and the second column satisfies \(Ly=d-2m e_s\). The omitted \(t\)-row follows because both sides sum to zero. All solutions differ by a constant, so \(y=h^{(s)}-H_{t\to s}\mathbf1\). As \(h^{(s)}_s=0\), \(y_s=-H_{t\to s}\).

This establishes correctness for every connected unweighted graph, beyond the engine’s \(2\le n\le6\) bound.

### Contract-preserving implementation requirement

The Markov module should construct \(A_t\), degrees, and both right-hand sides independently from adjacency. It must not consume the resistance Laplacian or any resistance result. Batch elimination only shares the generic exact solver.

After solving, verify both original first-step systems exactly:

\[
d_vh^{(t)}_v-\sum_{w\sim v}h^{(t)}_w=d_v\quad(v\ne t),
\]

\[
d_vh^{(s)}_v-\sum_{w\sim v}h^{(s)}_w=d_v\quad(v\ne s),
\]

with the appropriate zero boundary. These residuals are complete certificates because each Dirichlet system has a unique solution.

### In-memory falsification results

No project files were written. Experiments used `uv run --no-project python` with the required D-drive cache.

- Every connected labelled simple graph on \(2\ldots6\) vertices, using the evaluator-selected edge: exact agreement with the existing two-solve implementation. This included all 26,704 connected labelled six-vertex graphs.
- Every ordered pair \(s\ne t\) on every connected labelled graph with \(2\ldots5\) vertices: 15,042 exact matches, zero failures.
- This automatically covered paths, stars, bridges, cut vertices, cycles, cliques, dense irregular graphs, asymmetric hitting times, and non-edge terminals.
- Every proposed result also passed the direct exact residual checks.

The most likely implementation errors are an incorrect sign in `-y[source]`, failing to shift the reverse vector by `y[source]`, or assuming the omitted grounded row holds without checking the right-hand side sums to zero.

### Arithmetic and timing evidence

Counting each pivot-row `Fraction` division, multiplication, and subtraction in the current Gauss–Jordan shape as one arithmetic operation:

| \(n\) | Connected graphs | Existing two solves | Proposed batch solve | Ratio |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2 | 1 | 4 | 3 | 1.333× |
| 3 | 4 | 108 | 64 | 1.688× |
| 4 | 38 | 3,272 | 1,870 | 1.750× |
| 5 | 728 | 145,880 | 81,840 | 1.782× |
| 6 | 26,704 | 10,520,904 | 5,830,888 | 1.804× |

For \(k=n-1\), factorization-plus-solves changes from two \(O(k^3)\) eliminations to one \(O(k^3)\) elimination with two \(O(k^2)\) right-hand sides. This is arithmetic-operation complexity; exact bit complexity remains dependent on intermediate numerator and denominator sizes.

On Python 3.13.7, Windows 10, 771 graphs per pass:

- Markov component, 4 warm-ups and 30 alternating measured passes:
  - existing median 171.788 ms, IQR 160.828–174.910 ms;
  - proposed median 114.147 ms, IQR 108.748–117.130 ms;
  - provisional median speedup 1.505×.
- Full analyzer prototype, 3 warm-ups and 20 alternating passes:
  - existing median 295.408 ms;
  - proposed median 243.429 ms;
  - provisional median speedup 1.214×;
  - complete returned dictionaries compared equal.

These are author-run, transcript-retained measurements, not an independent benchmark certification.

### Prior art and novelty

The mathematical ingredients are established:

- Sidford’s lecture notes derive \(Lh=d-\lVert d\rVert_1e_t\), gauge invariance, and the pseudoinverse hitting-time formula: [Stanford CME 305 Lecture 13](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cme305/Files/l13.pdf).
- Generalized inverses have long been used to recover whole mean-first-passage matrices: [Meyer, 1975](https://benisrael.net/MEYER-GROUP-INVERSE-76.pdf) and [Hunter, 1982](https://doi.org/10.1016/0024-3795(82)90218-X).
- Tetali gives one-way hitting times through effective resistances: [Tetali, 1991](https://tetali.math.gatech.edu/PUBLIS/pt4.pdf).
- Chandra et al. establish the commute-time identity: [Chandra et al.](https://homes.cs.washington.edu/~ruzzo/papers/resist.pdf).
- Reusing one elimination or factorization for multiple right-hand sides is standard linear algebra.

A targeted search did not locate this exact minimal arrangement—ground at \(t\), solve the forward and gauge-shifted reverse Poisson columns together, retain resistance independence, and certify both with exact residuals—but general pseudoinverse methods plainly subsume it. Another independent discovery branch also reached the paired-solve idea.

The defensible claim is therefore: **a project-specific exact optimization of the Atlas workload, apparently absent from the current engine, with a short proof and exhaustive bounded falsification**. It is not defensible as a new random-walk theorem or globally novel linear-algebra method. An independent verifier would still need to inspect the implementation and rerun canonical artifacts before promotion.
